question: A 38-year-old man has a tibial shaft fracture at 9 months with abundant callus bridging the fracture ends on plain radiograph, but no clinical union. Which Weber-Cech type is this, and what is the first-line management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Atrophic non-union shows absent callus, indicating poor biological potential; this case has abundant bridging callus.

answers.text: Hypertrophic non-union — responds to mechanical stability (e.g., nail exchange or compression plating)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hypertrophic non-union has good biological potential (ample callus) but lacks mechanical stability; compression or intramedullary nailing provides the missing stability without the need for graft.
Infected non-union is suspected when there is a draining sinus, elevated CRP/ESR, or organisms on biopsy; abundant callus alone does not indicate infection.
Oligotrophic non-union has minimal callus but retains some biological potential; it is not described by abundant bridging callus and is not the first-line scenario here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review Weber-Cech classification: hypertrophic (elephant foot/horse hoof) has callus but lacks rigidity; atrophic has no callus and needs both biology and stability.
Well done. Abundant callus = hypertrophic non-union = biological potential intact → mechanical stability is the cure.
